text: Lesson 1 established what an Internal Developer Platform is for: absorbing cognitive load that would otherwise sit on every stream-aligned team. This lesson is about how a platform team has to actually run in order to deliver that, because building the right capability once and never touching it again doesn't work — needs change, and a platform that stops adapting to its users quietly turns into the same brittle infrastructure it was supposed to replace.

In this model, the stream-aligned teams who use the platform are its customers, not a population it regulates. That reframing matters because a platform team that ignores what its customers need doesn't lose them the way an external product would — there's rarely a competing internal platform to switch to. Instead, it loses them to shadow infrastructure: developers quietly building their own workarounds. Usage numbers can look fine on a dashboard while real adoption is quietly collapsing underneath them.

Product thinking is the corrective, and it looks concrete, not aspirational: real user research instead of guesswork about what's slowing teams down, a roadmap prioritized by actual developer pain points rather than whatever's technically interesting to build, feedback channels that visibly change outcomes instead of disappearing into a backlog, and iteration after launch — a golden path template ships as a first version, not a finished artifact, and gets revised based on how teams actually use it.

Team Topologies names the interaction mode this requires: X-as-a-Service. The platform exposes a well-defined, self-service interface — an API, a template, a portal — that other teams consume directly, with minimal ongoing hand-holding. That's deliberately different from collaboration mode, where two teams work closely on a shared problem. X-as-a-Service only works if the interface itself is good enough that teams don't need to escalate to a human every time.

Which is exactly why the feedback loop from this lesson isn't optional polish — it's the mechanism that keeps the self-service interface good enough to hold up under real use. Next, this chapter gets specific about what the platform team actually ships first: golden paths, the supported, opinionated default way to build and deploy a service, and why that beats handing every team unlimited freedom.
